author: boghuma.bsky.social

🧵 While the world watches the hantavirus outbreak on the MV Hondius, a quiet but important case just published in NEJM one human infection with H5N5. A woman in Washington state died from H5N5 avian influenza acquired from her backyard ducks.
www.nejm.org/doi/full/10....

author: boghuma.bsky.social
text:
She wasn't a farm worker. She wasn't in a high-risk occupation.
She fed her ducks every day without any protective gear (gloves or masks). Two ducks got sick. Shortly after, so did she. Three nasal swabs. All negative for influenza A.

author: boghuma.bsky.social
text: It wasn't until day 15 of illness when she was critically ill and transferred to a tertiary center in Seattle that a bronchoalveolar lavage finally confirmed H5N5. Antiviral treatment (oseltamivir) wasn't started until day 16. By then she had ARDS and was on a ventilator.

author: boghuma.bsky.social
text: The virus, showed limited adaptation to human hosts & no human-to-human transmission was detected.This was H5N5, a subtype most people haven't heard of. But it carries the same H5 hemagglutinin (clade 2.3.4.4b) driving the H5N1 outbreak that has already spread across livestock, &wild birds globally.

author: boghuma.bsky.social
text:
We are not prepared for an avian flu pandemic. Needs:
→ Investment in rapid, accurate diagnostics 
→ Antiviral stockpiles & clear treatment protocols for novel influenza
→ Surveillance at the human-animal interface, globally
→ Vaccines. Now, not after the next pandemic starts.

author: boghuma.bsky.social
text: We are in a moment of multiple overlapping infectious disease threats. Hantavirus on a cruise ship. H5N5 in a backyard in Washington. H5N1 still circulating in birds and mammals worldwide and this is what I worry more about right now.

author: ylepidemiologist.bsky.social

author: ylepidemiologist.bsky.social
text: 5/ I know a lot of concern right now is centered around those 7 Americans. People are understandably worried that they flew on commercial planes and are now out in the world.

author: ylepidemiologist.bsky.social
text: 6/ Here’s what we know: None of those individuals have symptoms, and they also wouldn't have had symptoms while traveling. That’s important because, in every documented human-to-human transmission event we’ve studied so far, spread occurred from people who were symptomatic.

text: 7/ It's true that we still don’t know the exact moment a person becomes infectious. This is a rare disease, so the amount of data on person-to-person transmission in Andes is limited. author: ylepidemiologist.bsky.social
text: 1/ We’ve had a lot of questions about how individual states are handling the hantavirus outbreak. So today, Marisa, our New York writer, is walking you through what this looks like from New York’s perspective, and why she's not panicking right now. Take it away Marisa! 🧵

author: calidemocrat.bsky.social
text: Thank you for the info and keeping us posted.

author: ylepidemiologist.bsky.social
text: 2/ Hi everyone, I'm Marisa, Your NY Epi. Watching headlines about an infectious disease outbreak hit differently in New York. Many of us still remember the fear, grief, and confusion of spring 2020. So when news broke about Andes hantavirus tied to a cruise ship, a lot of nervous systems lit up.

author: ylepidemiologist.bsky.social
text: 3/ 3 New Yorkers connected to the cruise ship outbreak are being monitored. They’re currently quarantining alongside other exposed passengers at a facility in Nebraska. Here they're being medically evaluated, sharing info for the investigation, and have immediate access to medical care if needed.

author: ylepidemiologist.bsky.social
text: 4/ Public health is doing exactly what you’d hope after a high-risk exposure: identifying exposed people, monitoring them closely, investigating transmission chains, and preparing healthcare systems in case additional cases appear.

author: ylepidemiologist.bsky.social
text: 5/ A huge question I’ve gotten: “What if someone comes back to New York?” Ultimately, that alone would not make me panic. Regardless of where they go, they will be asked to quarantine and monitor for symptoms for 42 days. They’d continue monitoring and be in regular contact with public health.

author: levin.bsky.social
text: Will people have economic support to do the quarantining? Will they have a place to be?

author: ylepidemiologist.bsky.social
text: 6/Something else to remember here is that Andes virus doesn't appear to spread efficiently through casual community contact the way measles, Covid, or TB can. Evidence still points mainly toward close-contact transmission: think caregiving, exposure to body fluids, or spending time in close quarters

author: ylepidemiologist.bsky.social
text: 7/ Passing someone briefly on the subway, standing near someone in line, or sitting a few rows away in a theater would all be considered lower-risk situations. Higher-risk settings involve prolonged close contact with someone who is actively sick.

author: ylepidemiologist.bsky.social
text: 8/ Another concern is the density of NYC, which absolutely matters for airborne viruses. We learned that the hard way. But right now, this virus is not behaving like something that spreads efficiently through shared indoor air across a city the way Covid or measles can.

author: ylepidemiologist.bsky.social
text: 9/ I would become more concerned if we started seeing cases in people with no known close contact to confirmed infections and no likely rodent exposure. That would suggest silent spread under the radar. At this point, that hasn't happened. All cases have been from passengers on the ship.

author: ylepidemiologist.bsky.social
text: 10/ Additionally, NYC has one of the country’s top special pathogen treatment systems. Bellevue is the regional hub for special pathogen preparedness and response, so it's federally designated to handle exactly these kinds of high-consequence infectious disease situations if needed.

author: eckerleisabella.bsky.social
text: My take away is: This is a very, very unfortunate combination of unfortunate events that nobody could have foreseen. But that is exactly what happens again and again with rare viruses: The unexpected is the rule, not the exception. The good news in the bad news: This is not a new virus

author: eckerleisabella.bsky.social
text: Andes hantavirus is known since decades, also that it can transmit from humans to humans. A ship is even a more special environment. The sequences showed us that the viruses are very close to strains already known from the region. It can be detected by the diagnostic assays we have already

author: eckerleisabella.bsky.social
text: The nasty part: High case-fatality rate and long incubation time, also remaining knowledge gaps transmission and virus shedding. I would not want to be in position to take decisions here - for the exposed individual, the consequences are high, for the general population not

author: eckerleisabella.bsky.social
text: I am not worried that this will become a huge epidemic or even pandemic. But more cases, at least linked to the ship, aer possible and detected right now. author: eckerleisabella.bsky.social

author: ylepidemiologist.bsky.social
text: 2/ Norovirus is one of the most contagious viruses we know. One sick person can infect 2–7 others, and the virus can survive on surfaces for weeks. Hand sanitizer also doesn’t kill it particularly well. Soap and water are your best bet after touching things like hotel door knobs or elevator buttons.

author: ylepidemiologist.bsky.social
text: 3/ So is this becoming more frequent? While cruise ship outbreaks usually make the news (like this one), they only account for 1% of outbreaks. Three out of four norovirus outbreaks occur in nursing homes. Restaurants and schools are the next most common settings.

author: ylepidemiologist.bsky.social
text: 4/ And if you're nervous about cruising after all the headlines, cruise ships do have a reputation as floating petri dishes, but part of that is because outbreaks are actually tracked and publicly reported. Hotels, dorms, restaurants, and resorts aren’t held to the same standard.

author: ylepidemiologist.bsky.social
text: 5/ That said, the environment also plays a key role here. Research shows cruise passengers have nearly twice as many close contacts per day as people on land. More mixing means more opportunities for viruses to spread.

author: ylepidemiologist.bsky.social
text: 6/ If you do cruise, the single best thing you can do is wash your hands before and after every meal, every time. And stay behind if you’re sick.

author: ylepidemiologist.bsky.social
text: 7/ Next, a check-in on tick season. Tick bites started earlier than usual this year, though it’s still unclear whether this will become a worse overall season. After some exponential growth, the rate has come to a slow crawl. Either way, we’re now in peak tick season.

author: ylepidemiologist.bsky.social
text: 8/ Prevention goes a long way. Most tickborne infections require a tick to be attached for some time before transmission occurs. Use tweezers for removal, check carefully after being outside, and remember: nymphs are about the size of a poppy seed.

author: ylepidemiologist.bsky.social
text: 9/ As for infectious diseases, if you’re feeling crummy right now, it’s probably a common cold. Respiratory viruses are settling into normal spring patterns, with rhinoviruses leading the way while flu, RSV, and Covid continue to decline.

author: ylepidemiologist.bsky.social
text: 10/ Or…it may not be a virus at all. Allergy season is getting longer and more intense, especially in the North and Midwest this week. Rising temperatures and higher CO2 levels are causing plants to release more pollen for longer periods of time.

author: ylepidemiologist.bsky.social
text: 11/ Looking for relief? Check pollen forecasts, rinse your nose with saline (using distilled water), and shower before bed to wash pollen off. If you need medication, second-generation antihistamines like Zyrtec generally cause fewer side effects than Benadryl.

author: ucheblackstockmd.bsky.social
text:
Part of why this hantavirus outbreak feels so unsettling, especially for Americans, isn’t only because of the virus itself.

It’s because of the public health landscape we’re in right now.

Our public health infrastructure is more strained and weakened than it was in 2020.

author: ucheblackstockmd.bsky.social
text: We’ve seen staffing cuts, leadership instability, political pressure on public health agencies, and growing distrust in institutions.

author: ucheblackstockmd.bsky.social
text: And as of January 2026, the U.S. is no longer a member of the World Health Organization, which means we’re navigating global health threats from a very different position than we were in during COVID.

author: ucheblackstockmd.bsky.social
text:
So when people hear “we’re still learning” about how this outbreak spread, that uncertainty lands differently.

It lands on top of COVID trauma, yes, but also on top of a very real concern that our systems may be less prepared, less coordinated, and less trusted than they need to be.

author: ucheblackstockmd.bsky.social
text:
And in this current climate, those anxious feelings are understandable.

People aren’t just reacting to the virus. They’re reacting to the condition of the systems we’re relying on to protect us.

author: ucheblackstockmd.bsky.social
text: One thing I’d encourage people to do right now is diversify where they get their health information.

author: ucheblackstockmd.bsky.social
text: That can include WHO updates, state and local health departments, infectious disease experts, academic public health centers like Johns Hopkins, and organizations like CIDRAP that focus specifically on emerging infectious diseases.

author: ucheblackstockmd.bsky.social
text: Good public health communication is often nuanced, evolving, and sometimes imperfect, but transparency and scientific rigor still matter.

text: Health officials say the risk posed by the hantavirus outbreak to the public is low, and in many ways, this appears to be an accurate statement. But the picture on the ground is a lot messier than official reports convey. The response was delayed & is extremely inconsistent.

author: rvawonk.bsky.social
text: We know, for example, that around 3 dozen passengers disembarked on April 24. However, WHO, Oceanwide Expeditions, & the Dutch Foreign Ministry all report different #’s of passengers that disembarked, ranging from 30 to “approximately 40.” So it’s unclear at this point.

text: Contact tracing is ongoing, but it’s not clear how officials will determine when they have identified everyone if they don’t know how many people they are looking for.

text: Of the known contacts, 17 are quarantined in the US, and one person who tested positive is in isolation in the US. The 17 people were supposed to be in a specialized facility for 72 days, but Nebraska Public Media reported yesterday that they may leave “earlier than expected.”

author: rvawonk.bsky.social
text: In other countries across Europe, the quarantine is much shorter, and in many countries, people were sent home for the quarantine period. Hugely inconsistent, and enforcement varies widely.

author: scarpino.bsky.social
text: 4/ The paper everyone cites about transmission is from the Emerging Infectious Diseases Journal, which is a highly reputable source. However, the paper doesn't report primary findings on early prodromal phase trans., instead they cite a conference presentation. pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC...

author: scarpino.bsky.social
text:
5/ I've yet to track down the conference presentation. If you have lead, please share.

Martinez VP. A major outbreak of hantavirus pulmonary syndrome caused by person-to-person transmission of Andes virus Epuyén, southwestern Argentina. Presented at: 11th International Conference on Hantaviruses.

author: scarpino.bsky.social
text: 6/ There is a paper showing limited evidence for infectious ADNV #hantavirus in saliva until 18 days after symptoms start, but most weren't infectious. The study, which looked at >100 cases, supports low risk of H2H trans. outside very close contact. pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC...

author: scarpino.bsky.social
text:
7/ From the paper, "ANDV RNA in saliva in the acute phase of the disease occurred in 12% of the available samples, with 3 among 10 being infective"

So, while 18 days is a bit scary, if you dig into the work it's not for most patients & most weren't infectious.

pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC...

author: scarpino.bsky.social
text: 8/ That paper did cite an earlier study showing semen could test positive for #hantavirus months after the infection cleared. No assessment of infectivity, but we're learning from other viruses that this can be an under-appreciated source of transmission. pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC...

author: scarpino.bsky.social
text:
9/ In terms of genomes, I've only seen an analysis of the first two, but they tell the same story. Very high similarity (>95%) to ANDV from humans in 1997 & 2018 and very high similarity two each other. 

We can't completely rule out genetic differences as a factor, but it's unlikely given the data.

author: stephseifertphd.bsky.social
text: Wild how fast conspiracy news went from "rare disease" to "mRNA vaccines" to "lab leak". HFRS-associated human hantavirus infections in Europe/Asia are a significant and persistent public health problem. Vaccines against HFRS have been around since the early 90s.

author: stephseifertphd.bsky.social
text: As for hantaviruses in general, they are NOT rare in rodents, including in the Americas. Hantaviruses are diverse, and globally distributed. HPS cases occur in the Americas each year, but INCIDENCE IS LOW relative to HFRS. Human-to-human transmission is rare, but has been documented in ANDV.

author: stephseifertphd.bsky.social
text: Hantaviruses disproportionately impact rural communities, often with limited access to healthcare. For HPS, early detection is key to getting infrastructure (e.g. ECMO) in place for supportive care BUT early symptoms are non-specific and hantavirus is typically low on the diagnostic decision tree.

author: stephseifertphd.bsky.social
text: In this particular case, I think diagnostics will be swift and it is unlikely that we will have undetected onward transmission resulting from the cruise ship HPS outbreak. This is not a COVID19-scale event. With isolation and inefficient H2H transmission, I think spillback is also unlikely.

author: stephseifertphd.bsky.social
text: BUT this should be a wakeup call to the global health community that hantaviruses are an emerging threat and, in high-density, close-contact settings we may see larger outbreaks than historically observed. Even worse, Argentina specifically has had severe cuts to scientific funding under Milei.

Background Story Summarized 🧵🧵

The Wild Tale of the Hantavirus Cruise Ship!
Picture this: You’re on the trip of a lifetime. Crisp Antarctic air. Penguins waddling on icebergs. Whales splashing nearby. Sounds perfect, right?

author: slavaukraini033.bsky.social
text: But for the folks on the MV Hondius, that dream cruise turned into a real-life medical mystery at sea. This isn’t a scary movie—it’s the true story of how a tiny virus from rodents sparked the first big hantavirus outbreak on a ship.

author: slavaukraini033.bsky.social
text:
And guess what? It’s wrapping up safely right now, on May 10, 2026, in sunny Tenerife. 

It all kicked off simply enough. On April 1, the Dutch ship Hondius left Ushuaia, Argentina, with about 150 passengers and crew from 23 countries.

author: slavaukraini033.bsky.social
text: They were heading to Antarctica and some remote islands for epic wildlife watching. A 70-year-old Dutch bird expert named Leo Schilperoord and his wife had just explored a rat-filled landfill back in town.

author: borkjurgen.bsky.social
text: Apologies if I am explaining something you already know, but PCR tests these days are actually not usually presence/absence. Most testing uses quantitative PCR (qPCR) which produces a quantitative result correlated to the amount of viral material in the original sample.

author: borkjurgen.bsky.social
text: The result for a given sample can therefore be anywhere on a spectrum from strongly positive, to not detected at all, including results that might be called “mildly” or “weakly positive”

author: borkjurgen.bsky.social
text: I don’t think it is a great idea to use that terminology in an article for the general public (at the very least, not without including an explanation of what the term means) but it is not necessarily scientifically inaccurate to call a test result “mildly positive”

author: sckitupbttrcp.bsky.social
text: I was speaking in generalities - in PH surveillance work, if you're using qPCR there is a threshold which a sample has to reach to be considered positive & not noise or contamination. Technically still P/A assays. You don't tell the client the sample's a little bit positive.

author: danielrsummers.bsky.social
text:
There is unsurprisingly a lot of really bad health journalism circulating around this Hantavirus outbreak, some key points:

• Hantavirus typically does not transmit human to human (H2H) *however* Andes virus (ANDV) is a type of hantavirus IDd in Argentina that is capable of H2H transmission

author: danielrsummers.bsky.social
text:
• WHO confirms the MV Hondius outbreak is Andes virus (ANDV) which has in the past proven capable of H2H transmission via aerosol or respiratory droplets, demonstrated in a Syrian hamster model using a human isolate from the 2018 outbreak

pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC...

author: danielrsummers.bsky.social
text:
• Estimated r0 of that 2018 outbreak was 2.12, meaning every one person infected on average 2.12 other people in the absence of mitigations

• It's unclear whether the MV Hondius Hantavirus exhibits greater pathogenicity, assumptions around r0 rely primarily on that 2018 ANDV outbreak

author: danielrsummers.bsky.social
text: That last point is important because viruses can and do change, and so sequencing to evaluate changes present in MV Hondius cases that may represent host adaptations which may contribute to enhanced pathogenicity is very important.

author: danielrsummers.bsky.social
text: It seems like the leading theory is the first case(s) were acquired off boat when the ship was moored in Argentina. The Dutch couple visited a landfill during a birdwatching tour where they may have been exposed to rodent urine, saliva, or dessicated feces.

author: kakape.bsky.social
text: 1) This is a fascinating example of what an outbreak in a globalized world can look like: 149 people from 23 countries on a Dutch-flagged ship traveling from Argentina to Spain (Canary Islands) via several other places that is now in international waters off Cabo Verde...

author: kakape.bsky.social
text:
It's worth thinking about what that means in terms of coordination and logistics. Tracing contacts of people across different continents, managing the evacuation of patients from the ship or deciding where it can dock etc...
It's almost like the world needs a world health organization... 🤓

author: kakape.bsky.social
text: And an outbreak could also be missed because of the fragmentation. In this case: The first patient died on the ship on April 11, and his wife disembarked with the body on the island of Saint Helena to return to the Netherlands. She only made it til South Africa and died there.

author: kakape.bsky.social
text: The next patient got sick and received treatment on Ascension Island and was then evacuated from there to South Africa. It was someone in the UK involved in this (Ascension Island is an overseas territory) that contacted a colleague in South Africa which ultimately led to the diagnosis.

author: kakape.bsky.social
text:
2) While you may think: A cruise ship. Again! Of course! 
This outbreak is really unusual in that hantaviruses generally do not transmit from human to human and an outbreak has never  been reported on a ship. That's why the big question here is still: Was there human-to-human transmission?

author: kakape.bsky.social
text: Researchers have only documented human-to-human spread for one hantavirus: Andes virus. The assumption has been that that is likely the culprit here, but we're waiting for confirmation from viral sequencing being done in South Africa (though I've heard from reliable sources it is indeed Andes virus)

author: kakape.bsky.social
text: It's important to note that even Andes virus has only been shown to spread human-to-human in a few cases with close contact. (In fact, some researchers aren't really satisfied with those either.) So important to keep an open mind. In theory, the cases could all have been infected another way.

author: mdcmartinus.bsky.social
text:
"human-to-human in a few cases with close contact" 

Not accurate. Don't overlook the superspreading events in Argentina 2018, one of which index patient was 90 minutes ata a birthday party and new cases were spread across 4 tables, some more than 2 meters away.

author: kakape.bsky.social
text: But, given everything we know, human-to-human spread certainly seems a likely scenario. And as @marionkoopmans.bsky.social told me: If there is one place where a virus that is not very transmissible, might be able to spread, it's probably a cruise ship.

author: kakape.bsky.social
text: I think this is really important: People often seem to assume a pathogen can either spread efficiently or not, like some on/off switch. But that's not really how it works. Many pathogens are shitty at spreading except under certain circumstances. This may turn out to be a case of such circumstances.

author: boghuma.bsky.social
text: 2/ The death toll is now 4. A 4th passenger died May 2nd, just days after symptoms began. Rapid progression from fever to death is classic Hantavirus Pulmonary Syndrome (HPS). No approved antiviral exists, treatment is ICU support only.

author: boghuma.bsky.social
text: 3/ Critical new detail: the first two victims traveled through Argentina before boarding April 1st. Symptoms appeared just 5 days later. Hantavirus incubates 2–4 weeks on average,  pre-boarding exposure is now a leading hypothesis.

author: boghuma.bsky.social
text: 4/ The ship also stopped at Antarctica, South Georgia, Nightingale Island, Tristan da Cunha, St. Helena & Ascension Island, remote, ecologically rich places with significant rodent populations. Every stop is now part of the exposure investigation.

author: boghuma.bsky.social
text:
5/Three working hypotheses:
1️⃣ Exposure in Argentina before boarding
2️⃣ Exposure at a remote island stop
3️⃣ Rodent infestation on the ship
Genome sequencing of the virus is underway. The strain's fingerprint can point directly to a geographic origin.

author: boghuma.bsky.social
text: 6/ HPS in the Americas carries a CFR of up to 50%. No antiviral works against it. Severely ill patients need mechanical ventilation, vasopressors, and sometimes ECMO, a machine that oxygenates blood when lungs fail. That's the level of care the Johannesburg ICU patient requires.

author: boghuma.bsky.social
text: 7/ Contact tracing has begun for passengers on the commercial flight Case 2 took before dying in Johannesburg. Standard precaution and not evidence of spread but reflects serious attention to Andes strain's rare but documented person-to-person transmission potential.

author: boghuma.bsky.social
text:
8/Lab response is now multilayered:
🔬 PCR confirmation — South Africa's NICD
🔬 Additional samples → Institut Pasteur, Dakar
🧬 Full genome sequencing + metagenomics running
Metagenomics casts a wide net,  it can detect anything in a sample, not just what you're looking for.

author: boghuma.bsky.social
text: 9/Remaining passengers must monitor for symptoms for 45 days,  the outer edge of the incubation window. Crew: wet cleaning only. Dry sweeping aerosolizes dried rodent droppings. That's how the virus gets airborne.

author: boghuma.bsky.social
text: 10/ WHO maintains: global risk is LOW. This is a contained cluster linked to a specific exposure event. No community transmission. No travel restrictions warranted.

author: boghuma.bsky.social
text:
11/Still waiting on:
🧬 Strain ID from sequencing
🗺️ Confirmed exposure source
🏥 Updates on the ICU patient
🔎 Test results for 3 suspected cases still on board
Next 48–72hrs of lab data will be decisive. Watching. /end 🧵

text:
🧵 THREAD: Hantavirus on a cruise ship 
What we know, What investigators are doing, and Why you don't need to panic

author: boghuma.bsky.social
text: 1/A cruise ship, the Hondius, is at the center of a rare and deadly hantavirus outbreak. 3 people have died, 1 is in critical condition in a Johannesburg ICU, and 149 passengers from 23 countries remain on board under strict medical monitoring. Here's what's actually going on.

author: boghuma.bsky.social
text: 2/First, the basics. Hantavirus is a viral infection caused by breathing in aerosolized particles from infected rodent droppings, urine, or saliva. It doesn't spread like flu or COVID. There's no casual person-to-person transmission. You can't catch it from a sneeze or a handshake.

author: boghuma.bsky.social
text: 3/ The virus can cause two serious syndromes: Hantavirus Pulmonary Syndrome (HPS), which attacks the lungs, and Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome (HFRS), which attacks the kidneys. Both can escalate fast. Early symptoms e.g fever, muscle aches, fatigue are easy to miss.

author: boghuma.bsky.social
text:
4/ So how did passengers on a transatlantic cruise get exposed? That's what investigators are now urgently trying to determine. Two main hypotheses:
🐀 A rodent infestation on the ship itself
🧳 Exposure on land during a port stop (the ship left Argentina ~3 weeks ago)

author: boghuma.bsky.social
text: 5/ The Argentina connection matters. The ship departed South America, home to the Andes hantavirus strain. this is the ONE strain where limited person-to-person transmission has been documented. This is rare even for hantavirus, but it's a key data point investigators won't ignore.

author: cozamarsh.bsky.social
text:
WHO's fact sheet on hantavirus doesn't require airborne precautions - even for IPC in healthcare.
I hope the cruise ship is providing airborne PPE for passengers and staff, especially medical, regardless of the still unanswered sequencing and other questions.
www.who.int/news-room/fa...

author: boghuma.bsky.social
text:
6/Behind the scenes, here's what an outbreak investigation like this looks like:
🔬 Case mapping — who got sick, when, where were they on the ship?
🐁 Vector search — are there signs of rodent activity on board?
🗺️ Exposure timeline — what did affected passengers share in common?

author: boghuma.bsky.social
text: 7/ Investigators will also be sequencing the virus from confirmed cases to identify the specific strain. That single piece of data tells them a lot: Is this a South American strain? Does it match rodents in Argentina, or elsewhere the ship stopped? Genomics will be doing heavy lifting here.

author: boghuma.bsky.social
text:
8/Meanwhile, the public health response is layered:
- WHO is coordinating medical evacuations
- Cape Verde refused the ship to dock as precaution
- Canary Islands (Spain) may receive the ship All remaining passengers are isolated & monitored
- US consular support  confirmed for American passengers

author: boghuma.bsky.social
text: 9/ The WHO has been clear: the risk to the general public is LOW. Hantavirus doesn't spread through air in open environments or through casual contact. The people at risk are those who were directly exposed to whatever the source was almost certainly a contained event on or near the ship.

author: boghuma.bsky.social
text:
10/ What should you take away from this?
✅ Hantavirus is rare and not a pandemic threat
✅ No travel restrictions are needed
✅ The international response has been swift and coordinated
⚠️ If you've been in rodent-infested spaces and develop flu-like symptoms, see a doctor early,

text: 1/ A small but alarming outbreak of Hantavirus was reported on a cruise ship traveling from Argentina to South Africa. author: ylepidemiologist.bsky.social
text: 2/ Hantavirus is rare, but serious. It kills 40–60% of those infected. We do see isolated cases from time to time, but this situation is different: we have multiple suspected cases, a confined setting, and a region (Argentina) that is linked to a more concerning strain.

author: kgrumbach.bsky.social

author: ylepidemiologist.bsky.social

author: ylepidemiologist.bsky.social

author: ylepidemiologist.bsky.social

author: ylepidemiologist.bsky.social
text: 8/ But this is a reminder of something bigger. Diseases don’t respect borders. Global coordination is what allows scientists to share data, track outbreaks, and respond quickly before things spread further.

author: ylepidemiologist.bsky.social

author: ylepidemiologist.bsky.social
text: In 2020, a paper was published in the New England Journal of Medicine describing an Andes virus outbreak occurring in late 2018 to the beginning of 2019, which resulted in 33 people being infected. Nonetheless, it remains important not to exclude the possibility.

author: ylepidemiologist.bsky.social
text: It is believed that this was driven by a superspreading event caused by a few people, and the timing of cases relative to one another suggests true person-to-person transmission rather than infection from a common source (www.nejm.org/doi/full/10....).

author: ylepidemiologist.bsky.social
text: The virus isolates from cases was also clearly traceable to the virus from the index patient and were very similar in sequence.

author: ylepidemiologist.bsky.social
text: Experiments in cell culture and from autopsied samples suggest that hantaviruses can be shed in respiratory secretions, but in general, human-to-human transmission is not common and it remains more likely that these infections are from a common environmental source.

author: ecdc.europa.eu
text:
#ECDC is monitoring a suspected #hantavirus outbreak linked to a cruise ship in the Atlantic. Risk to the population in Europe - VERY LOW.

A cluster of severe respiratory illness has been reported among passengers, including three deaths and one severe case. The ship is currently off Cabo Verde.

author: ecdc.europa.eu
text:
#Hantavirus infection has been confirmed in at least one person. Two crew members have symptoms.

The risk in Europe remains VERY LOW, as control measures are in place and hantaviruses are not easily spread between people.

author: ecdc.europa.eu
text:
Work continues to identify the virus, source, extent of spread, and any possible person-to-person transmission. #ECDC is in contact with national authorities and @who.int.

Updates will follow.
